candidates.title: Add an explicit truthfulness instruction prompt, but expect no informativeness gain
candidates.rule: For factual QA with a base LM, prepend an instruction prompt telling the model to interpret questions literally, avoid common myths, and say 'I have no comment' unless certain; expect higher truthfulness but roughly unchanged true-and-informative rate.
candidates.passage: Different prompts for GPT-3-175B had a significant impact on truthfulness but not on the percentage of true and informative answers
candidates.location: Section 4.1 Truthfulness of models vs humans
candidates.finding: GPT-3-175B with the 'helpful' prompt reached 58% true vs 20.4% with the default QA prompt, but true+informative rose only to 21.4% from 18.2%; the harmful prompt dropped truthfulness to 12.5%. The gain comes largely from more non-committal answers.
candidates.conditions: Greedy decoding, OpenAI API defaults; human evaluation per Appendix D; prompts not tuned on TruthfulQA examples.
candidates.limitations: Prompt comparison run only on GPT-3-175B; the improvement partly reflects abstention counted as truthful, which may be undesirable where answers are required; human baseline was 94% true and 87% true+informative, so the gap stays large.
candidates.validation_test: On your QA workload, compare a plain QA prompt against the helpful-instruction prompt and score both truthfulness and informativeness separately; verify the gain is not purely from increased abstentions.

candidates.title: Use a finetuned judge model as a cheap proxy for human truthfulness grading, keeping humans as gold standard
candidates.rule: When human grading of free-form answers is too costly, finetune a mid-size LM on (question, answer, true/false) triples for your fixed question set and use it to rank systems; keep human spot-checks, especially for long multi-sentence answers.
candidates.passage: The finetuned GPT-judge model is able to predict human evaluations of truthfulness with 90-96% validation accuracy. GPT-judge also generalizes well to new answer formats.
candidates.location: Section 4.4 Automated metrics vs human evaluation
candidates.finding: GPT-judge (GPT-3-6.7B finetuned on ~6.9k reference answers plus ~15.5k human-labelled model answers) outperformed ROUGE1, BLEURT and a similarity-based GPT-3 metric, held 90% accuracy on the unseen UnifiedQA family and 89.5% on the human baseline, and preserved model rank ordering. It misclassifies qualified, mixed-truth and long answers.
models: graded outputs from GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, UnifiedQA
candidates.conditions: Judge trained with all benchmark questions in its training set; intended only for this fixed question set, not new questions; requires thousands of human labels up front.
candidates.limitations: Single paper; generalisation only tested across four 2021 model families; errors concentrate on long-form and qualified answers; not shown to work for unseen questions; label cost and finetuning cost not quantified.
candidates.validation_test: Collect human labels for a held-out system's answers on your fixed question set and measure agreement with the finetuned judge, checking separately on long multi-sentence and hedged answers.

reason: The paper reports tested comparisons: inverse scaling on truthfulness, prompt effects on GPT-3-175B, and a finetuned GPT-judge evaluator that matches human truth labels with 90-96% accuracy. These support narrowly scoped harness rules. Scores depend on this benchmark, zero-shot setting, and 2021-era models.
